lesson_title: The Patrol Nobody Would Pay For
hook_text: Your whole street wants the night patrol. Nobody will pay for it. Here's why — and who fixes it.
clip_script: Walk your street and sort everything into two piles. The vetkoek, the data bundle, the haircut — pay and it's yours. The market runs those perfectly. Now the night patrol the street keeps talking about. Once a patrol walks the block, the block is safer for EVERYONE — the nurse off shift, the shopkeeper cashing up, the child asleep by the window. Nobody can be left out of safety. So who volunteers to pay? Every house runs the same maths: if the neighbours pay, I'm protected free; if they don't, my money is wasted alone. Everyone waits for everyone — and the patrol never starts. That's the free-rider problem, and it's why safety, streetlights and storm drains are bought by all of us together, through tax, or not at all. But tax has a breaking point, and here's the twist. Tax the barber at the rank at zero percent: the state collects nothing. Tax him at a HUNDRED percent: he locks up and cuts hair at home for cash — the state still collects nothing. Somewhere between sits the rate that collects the most, and past that crest, squeezing harder collects LESS. That hump is the Laffer curve. The state needs your rand — and needs to know when to stop asking.
visual_style: A dusk street where windows glow with faces waiting for each other while a patrol lantern stays dark; coins finally stream into a shared pot and the lantern lights, then the pot morphs into a rising-and-falling revenue hump over a barbershop pole.
mood: Wry and thoughtful, ending on a clean punchline.
pacing: Patient through the waiting-windows standoff, a satisfying snap as the lantern lights, brisk over the hump.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and carry the free-rider, the budget and the Laffer curve into any economics essay.
